name: Marcus Rashford
label: Free school meals campaign
why: His open letters and campaign forced two UK government reversals in 2020, extending free school meal support (GBP 120m in June, GBP 170m winter package in November) reaching about 1.3-1.7 million children. A national policy change, well beyond the foundation-level giving Character credits.

name: Sócrates
label: Corinthians Democracy
why: Led the player-run Corinthians Democracy under Brazil's military regime, with 'Dia 15 Vote' shirts before the 1982 elections, then spoke at Diretas Já rallies. Open political defiance of a dictatorship at personal risk.

name: Didier Drogba
label: Ivory Coast peace plea
why: After World Cup qualification in October 2005 he led a televised dressing-room plea for both sides to lay down arms, credited with helping bring a ceasefire and renewed talks (the truce later broke down). His foundation also funds a hospital in Abidjan.

name: Just Fontaine
label: Founded French players' union
why: Co-founded the UNFP in 1961 and was its first president; its fight against lifetime contracts tying players to clubs led to the fixed-term 'contrat a temps' (1968-69), still in force. A lasting change for every French professional.

name: Raymond Kopa
label: 'Footballers are slaves' stand
why: As France's biggest star he publicly called players 'slaves' of lifetime contracts and received a suspended six-month ban; the campaign he backed with the UNFP won fixed-term contracts in 1968-69. Spoke out at real career risk.

name: Neven Subotić
label: Wells and sanitation in East Africa
why: His foundation (now well:fair) has completed more than 500 water and sanitation projects in Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania, serving over 400,000 people, and he has given up much of a pro lifestyle to run it. Measurable impact beyond a typical player foundation.

name: Megan Rapinoe
label: Equal pay and anthem stand
why: A leading voice and named complainant in the USWNT equal-pay fight that ended in the 2022 $24m settlement and the first equal World Cup prize-money CBA; earlier knelt in 2016, was booed and prompted a US Soccer stand-for-the-anthem rule (repealed 2020). National impact plus real personal cost.

name: Alex Morgan
label: Lead plaintiff, USWNT equal pay
why: Named lead plaintiff in the 2019 suit (after the 2016 EEOC complaint) that produced the 2022 $24m settlement and equal pay, including World Cup prize money, in the US Soccer CBAs; also pushed NWSL abuse accountability in 2021. Leading a fight with lasting national effect.

name: Becky Sauerbrunn
label: Led USWNT players' union to equal pay
why: EEOC complainant in 2016 and first USWNTPA president, signing the 2022 CBA with equal pay and equal World Cup prize money; publicly demanded NWSL owners step aside after the 2022 abuse report. Years of leadership beyond plaintiff status.

name: Christine Sinclair
label: Canada pay-equity fight to Parliament
why: As captain she led the players' 2023 dispute with Canada Soccer, including a threatened strike and testimony to the House of Commons heritage committee; the federation committed to equal per-match pay and shared World Cup prize money. Led at the end of her career with public risk.

name: Ada Hegerberg
label: Five-year Norway boycott
why: Stepped away from Norway for five years over the federation's treatment of the women's game, missing the 2019 World Cup as the reigning Ballon d'Or winner. A stand at real career cost.

name: Aitana Bonmatí
label: One of 'Las 15'
why: One of 15 Spain players who withdrew from selection in September 2022 over conditions under Vilda and the RFEF, facing heavy public criticism; after the 2023 Rubiales affair she again backed the players' stand that forced federation reform. Real career risk before the leadership changed.

name: Julie Foudy
label: Child-labour stand and pay holdout
why: Refused to rely on Reebok's word and inspected Sialkot ball factories for child labour in 1997, becoming the first woman and first American to win the FIFA Fair Play Award; led the 1995-96 pay holdout and later chaired the Women's Sports Foundation. Sustained leadership beyond peers.

name: Brandi Chastain
label: Safer Soccer heading campaign
why: Co-led the Safer Soccer campaign (Concussion Legacy Foundation) and pledged her brain to CTE research; in 2015 US Soccer banned heading for players 10 and under and limited it for 11-13. Shared credit with the campaign and a lawsuit, but a national rule change.

name: Johan Cruyff
label: Cruyff Foundation and Courts
why: His foundation has built hundreds of Cruyff Courts and school courts in more than 20 countries for children and disabled sport, and he founded the Cruyff Institute. Built and led a lasting movement beyond a typical foundation.

name: Patrick Vieira
label: Diambars academy, Senegal
why: Co-founded the Diambars institute in Saly, an education-first football school for Senegalese youth, running for over 20 years; also a persistent voice on racism and the lack of Black coaches. Decades of work beyond peers.

name: Javier Zanetti
label: Fundación PUPI
why: With his wife he has run Fundación PUPI for 25 years, providing food, education and health support to poor children in Buenos Aires Province and expanding to new centres; recognised at the UN. Sustained work clearly beyond peers.

name: Kenny Dalglish
label: Hillsborough support and cancer appeal
why: As Liverpool manager he and Marina attended funerals (four in one day) and supported families, a strain he named as the main reason he resigned in 1991; the Marina Dalglish Appeal (2004-05) has since raised over GBP 13m for cancer care on Merseyside.

name: Vinícius Júnior
label: Anti-racism fight in Spain
why: Repeatedly confronted racist abuse and pressed LaLiga and the courts; the Mestalla case brought the first racism convictions in Spanish professional football (2024), with him as a party. Stood up at real personal cost and with national effect; his Character penalties stand separately.

name: Landon Donovan
label: San Diego Loyal walk-offs
why: As coach he led two walk-offs in 2020 over a racist slur and a homophobic slur at Collin Martin; the second forfeit while leading 3-1 knocked the team out of playoff contention. A stand at clear sporting cost.

name: David Beckham
label: Twenty years with UNICEF
why: UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador since 2005; his 7 Fund (2015) has raised millions and reached over a million children, and he gave his 2013 PSG salary to a children's charity. Recognised with the 2025 WEF Crystal Award; sustained beyond peers.

name: Mohamed Salah
label: Rebuilding Nagrig
why: Has funded a school, hospital and medical units, an ambulance station, water treatment and monthly support for poor families in his home village, plus a Cairo children's cancer hospital. Sustained giving well beyond peers; reported figures vary.

name: George Weah
label: Funded Liberia's team in the civil war
why: Paid flights, kit, hotels and bonuses for the Liberia national team from his own pocket during and after the civil war, and worked with UNICEF; later conceded the 2023 presidential election peacefully. Sustained personal cost; the 2002 funding is disputed.
